transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Hello, Doctor. Well, I suppose... I mean, it's mostly because things at the store have been getting really difficult lately. I’m a floor supervisor in retail, have been doing it a long time, and I’ve always prided myself on my communication. I have my bachelor's degree, I know how to run a team, I know how to organize a stockroom. 

But I came in because recently, when I try to explain the inventory numbers to my staff, or even just going over the basic weekend schedule—which is a routine thing, I do it every single week—my words just start jumping all over the place. I'll start off talking about the delivery trucks, and then somehow I'm on to Thursdays, because of the delivery schedule, and then that brings up the church grill, and then I'm going on about my boss’s tone of voice... and it all connects in my head, it really does, the line from one thing to the next is right there. But I look at my team, the cashiers and the stock guys, and they just have these blank expressions. People look at me like they absolutely cannot follow what I’m saying. 

Like I'm speaking a completely different language or something. It’s incredibly frustrating because I know exactly what needs to be done on the floor, I know the numbers, but the instructions just pour out of my mouth in this big tangled web. And I can't seem to stop it from happening, no matter how hard I concentrate before the morning meetings. It's getting to the point where I'm dreading talking to my own crew.
When someone gives you directions or explains something, do you have trouble understanding what they mean?

Well, no, not exactly. I mean, when people talk to me, I hear the words perfectly fine. Like if my regional manager comes in and says we need to reorganize the endcaps by Tuesday because the new promotional items are shipping in early, I understand every single word of that sentence. The problem isn't my hearing or my comprehension, not at all. I can read the corporate memos, I can listen to the district conference calls—which are usually an hour long and incredibly dry, let me tell you, just droning on about quarterly projections and shrink percentages—and I follow all of it without a hitch. 

It's just... it's just when I try to respond, or when I'm the one who has to initiate the explanation. That's when the wires get crossed. But if someone is just giving me directions? Like, "Hey, can you move those pallets to the back room?" or "Did you check the security logs from last night?" I know exactly what they want. I might start thinking about the pallets, and how the wood on them always splinters, and how my grandfather used to do woodworking, and then I might try to say something about that when I answer them... but the actual understanding of what they asked me to do? No, that part is completely fine. I've never had an issue with following instructions, which is why it's so baffling that I can't seem to give them anymore.
Have you always had trouble having back-and-forth conversations with other people?

No, no, not always. I mean, like I said, I've been in retail management for a long time, and you just can't do this job if you can't talk to people. I used to be great at it. I could have a conversation with anyone—customers who were upset about a return policy, vendors trying to push extra product on us, the district managers who always want to see higher margins. I could banter with the cashiers during the slow hours, you know, just shooting the breeze about sports or what they were doing over the weekend. I was always the one people came to when there was a dispute on the floor because I could talk everyone down and figure out a solution. 

It really wasn't until recently that this... this tangling started happening. I used to be able to go back and forth, point for point, in a meeting without missing a beat. I remember a few years ago, we had a massive overhaul of the POS system, and I was the one training the entire front end. I was answering questions left and right, explaining the new touch screens, walking them through the new void procedures, and it was seamless. We went back and forth, they asked a question, I gave a direct answer. 

But now... now if someone asks me a question, even a simple one, I try to answer, and my brain just pulls in all these other things. Like if a cashier asks me if they can take their fifteen-minute break, I might start thinking about the time, and then the clock on the wall, and how the batteries in it need changing, and then I'm talking to them about alkaline batteries and the electronics aisle... and I completely lose the rhythm of the conversation. So, no, it definitely hasn't always been like this. It's a recent change, and it's just... it's exhausting, honestly. I used to love the social part of my job, and now I just feel like I'm constantly tripping over my own thoughts.
When someone is talking to you, do you ever struggle to understand the words they’re saying?

Well, like I was saying before, the words themselves aren't the issue. I mean, I hear the words clearly. If someone is standing right in front of me, looking me in the eye, and they say, "The truck is running late," I know exactly what those words mean. "Truck." "Running." "Late." The dictionary definitions of those words are perfectly intact in my brain. I don't sit there wondering what a truck is, or what it means to be late. 

It's not like I'm losing my vocabulary or anything like that. I read the newspaper every morning—well, I read the digital version on my tablet while I have my coffee, usually around 6:00 AM before I have to get ready for my shift—and I understand all the articles. The local news, the business section, even the opinion pieces. I understand the words just fine. 

So when someone is talking to me, no, I don't struggle to understand the actual words they are saying. The problem is never on the receiving end of the words, if that makes sense. It's only when I have to take those words, process them, and formulate my own response that everything just goes completely haywire. But just understanding what they are saying to me? No, that's not a problem at all. I hear them, I know what the words mean, and I know what they are trying to communicate to me.
Do you have this same difficulty speaking when you're alone or talking to someone you know very well, like a close family member?

Well, let me think about that. You would think it might be easier, right? Being with someone you're comfortable with. But my wife, for instance... we have been married for thirty-two years this coming October. She knows me better than absolutely anyone else on this earth. She knows my moods, she knows how I like my coffee—just black, no sugar, ever since I decided to cut back on sweets a decade ago—she just knows me inside and out. But even with her, sitting right there at our own kitchen table while we are having dinner, it still happens. 

I will try to tell her about something simple, maybe how the regional director is pushing the new store credit cards, and I want to explain the application quotas to her. But then I will look at the salt shaker on the table. And I start thinking about salt, and the ocean, and that vacation we took to the coast back in 2008, and suddenly I am talking to her about the tides and seagulls when I was trying to talk about credit applications. She just gets this very confused look on her face. 

And as for when I am alone... well, I do not talk out loud a whole lot when I am completely by myself, except maybe when I am driving. I have a forty-five-minute commute to the store, mostly highway, and sometimes I try to practice my morning huddle announcements out loud. Just me, the steering wheel, the radio turned all the way down. I will start saying to the empty car that we really need to focus on loss prevention today, but then the word loss makes me think of losing my keys, and then the locksmith who came to the house that one time, and his van, and the tires on his van... and even with nobody there to hear me, I completely lose the thread of my own sentence. I am just talking to the windshield about tire tread. 

So, honestly, I am not really sure if there is any difference at all. I haven't noticed one. It doesn't seem to matter who is in the room, or if there is anyone in the room at all. The wires just cross no matter what the situation is.
Did you have any similar trouble with speech, language, or communication as a child?

No, no, nothing like that when I was a kid. I mean, I grew up in a pretty standard household, you know? Two parents, an older sister who was always trying to boss me around, a dog named Buster. We lived in this split-level house in a neighborhood where all the kids played out in the street until the streetlights came on. And I was always right in the thick of it. I was a talkative kid, actually. My mother used to say I could talk the ear off a brass monkey. 

I remember in elementary school, I think it was third grade, Mrs. Gable's class, I actually won a little ribbon for a speech I gave about the solar system. I stood right up there in front of all the other kids and their parents—it was an open house night, so the room was packed—and I talked all about Jupiter and its moons. I didn't stumble over my words, I didn't get confused about what I was trying to say. I just delivered the information, plain and simple. 

And through middle school and high school, it was the same thing. I was on the debate team for a year in high school. I wasn't the star of the team or anything, but I could hold my own. We had to argue about things like school uniforms and funding for the arts, and I could structure an argument perfectly well. First point, second point, conclusion. Boom, boom, boom. 

Even in college, when I was getting my bachelor's degree—I majored in business administration, which is how I ended up in retail management, of course—I had to take a public speaking course. Everyone dreaded it, but I didn't mind it at all. I gave presentations on supply and demand, market saturation, all those dry economic concepts, and I never had any trouble keeping my thoughts straight. I could outline a speech, stand up, and deliver it exactly how I planned it in my head. 

So, no, as a child, as a teenager, as a young adult... my communication was always perfectly normal. Above average, even, I'd say, given my career path. This whole thing where my brain just splinters off into a dozen different directions when I try to finish a sentence... it's entirely new. It has no roots in my childhood at all. It's just... it's like a switch got flipped recently, and suddenly the wiring is all wrong. But back then? No, I was a perfectly articulate kid.
As a child, did you have trouble making or keeping friends?

No, no, I didn't have any trouble with that. Like I was saying about the neighborhood, there were always kids around. We had this big group of guys—Tommy, Ricky, Steve from two houses down—and we were always together. We built this massive fort in the woods behind Ricky's house one summer, must have been 1976 because I remember we had all these bicentennial flags we dragged out there. We spent weeks dragging scrap wood and old pallets out there. I was the one who kind of organized everybody, telling them where to put the nails, how to brace the walls so it wouldn't collapse on us. 

I was always the one organizing things, even back then. If we were playing kickball in the cul-de-sac, I was the one making the teams, making sure it was fair so nobody got upset and went home crying. I just had a knack for bringing people together, you know? And it stayed that way through school. I wasn't the captain of the football team or the prom king or anything like that, but I had a very solid, reliable group of friends. We went to dances together, we went to the movies on Friday nights... we'd go to the old Starlight drive-in before they tore it down in the late eighties to build that strip mall. 

And I kept those friends for a long time. Steve and I actually ended up going to the same college for a couple of years before he transferred out of state. I was the best man at his first wedding. So, making friends, keeping friends, talking to people, being part of a group... that was never an issue for me. I was always very social, very connected. I liked being around people, and people generally liked being around me. I was dependable. I still am dependable, really, at work and with my wife, it's just... well, it's just the talking part that's gotten so strange now. But as far as making friends went, no, I never struggled with that at all. It was always very natural for me.
Do you have any very strong, narrow interests or routines that you feel unusually attached to?

Well, let me think about what you mean by that. Strong interests or routines... I mean, I have a schedule, certainly. As a retail manager, you absolutely have to live by a schedule, or the whole operation just falls apart. I get up at 5:30 AM every single weekday. I make my coffee—like I told you, black, using that French press my wife got me for our twenty-fifth anniversary, which honestly makes a much better cup than those standard drip machines. Then I am at the store by 6:45. I unlock the front doors, I check the cash office, I make sure the registers have their starting drawers, and I review the daily sales goals before the morning huddle. 

But am I unusually attached to it? No, I really wouldn't say that. If corporate decides to change the opening procedure, which they actually did last spring when we upgraded all the point-of-sale systems... what a nightmare that transition week was, by the way. The new scanners were not reading half the barcodes on our seasonal clearance items, and I had customers lined up halfway to the fitting rooms. But anyway, when they change things, I just learn the new routine. It does not upset me or throw me into a panic. I just adapt to it.

And as for narrow interests... no, not really. I like perfectly normal things. I watch baseball, I follow the Braves, have since the nineties when they had that incredible pitching rotation. Sometimes I will read a historical biography. I read a very thick one on Teddy Roosevelt a few months ago. But I don't obsess over things. I don't collect stamps or spend all my time building model trains in the basement or anything like that. 

I just have my job, my wife, my house. I do like keeping the lawn looking nice, so I try to mow it every Sunday morning at 9 AM, unless it is raining, of course. You cannot mow wet grass, it just clumps up under the deck of the mower and then you are out there in the driveway with a putty knife scraping green sludge off the blades for an hour. But if it rains, I just wait until Monday evening. It doesn't bother me. So, no, no unusual attachments or narrow interests at all. Just a regular, everyday routine.
Were you like this with social communication and understanding social cues when you were a child, or did that seem normal until recently?

No, no, like I was saying before, everything was completely normal back then. I never had any trouble understanding people or... or figuring out what they meant when they didn't say it out loud, you know? Reading the room, I guess you'd call it. I was always very good at that, even as a little kid. 

I remember we had this neighbor, Mr. Henderson, who lived right on the corner of our street. He had this immaculate lawn, just perfect Kentucky bluegrass, and if our baseball ever went into his yard... well, you had to know exactly how to read his mood before you went to ask for it back. If he was sitting on his front porch smoking his pipe and his shoulders were relaxed, you were fine. You just walk up, say please and thank you, and he'd toss it back. But if he was out there pulling weeds and his jaw was set, or if he was aggressively coiling his garden hose, you just knew—you wait until tomorrow. You don't even approach him. I picked up on things like that instantly. I always knew when a teacher was having a bad day, or when my sister was actually mad versus when she was just pretending to be annoyed. 

And honestly, it's the exact same skill that made me good at my job. You simply cannot survive in retail management for thirty-odd years if you don't understand social cues. When a customer walks into the store, I can tell within five seconds if they want to be greeted and guided through the merchandise, or if they just want to be left entirely alone to browse. I can tell when a cashier is lying to me about why they were late for their shift, just by the way they won't hold eye contact or how they shift their weight from one foot to the other. I've built my whole career on understanding exactly what people mean and how to communicate with them effectively. 

So this... this whole situation now, where I'm talking and suddenly the words just don't connect the way they're supposed to, or I completely lose the thread of the conversation... it's completely out of left field. It didn't start until very recently. Before this, I was the guy everyone came to when they needed someone to smooth over a misunderstanding at the store, or de-escalate a situation with an angry customer. I was the diplomat. So, no, absolutely nothing like this when I was a child. I've always been perfectly tuned in to how people operate.
When you’re trying to speak, do you have trouble finding the right words?

Well, finding the right words... it's not exactly that I can't find them. They're all right there in my head. It's more about... what happens when I try to string them together. That's actually the whole reason I came in to see you in the first place. 

It happens at the store mostly. I'll be in the back room, or out on the floor before we open, and I'll be trying to explain the inventory numbers to my assistant manager, Dave. Dave's a good kid, he's been with us for about four years, but he really needs things spelled out clearly, especially when we're going over the weekend schedule. Weekends are our highest volume days, obviously, so everyone needs to know exactly where they're supposed to be. So, I'll start talking, trying to lay out the plan, and then my words just... they start jumping all over the place. 

I'll start off talking about the delivery trucks that are supposed to come in, and then suddenly I'm talking about Thursdays for some reason, and then before I even realize it, I'm going on about the church grill—because we had this big parish picnic a few weeks back and someone brought this massive industrial charcoal grill that just kept smoking out the entire pavilion—and then from there I'm suddenly talking about my boss's tone of voice on our last district conference call. 

And it all feels perfectly connected in my head while I'm saying it, like one thought naturally leads right into the next, but then I stop and look at Dave, or the cashiers, and they just have these blank expressions. They look at me like they absolutely cannot follow what I'm saying. Their eyebrows get all scrunched up, and they're just staring at me like I'm speaking a foreign language. It is incredibly frustrating, let me tell you, because like I said before, I have always been the communicator. I've always been the one to give clear directions. But now I open my mouth to talk about the seasonal endcaps, and somehow I end up on a complete tangent about a barbecue and my district manager's attitude, and my whole team is just standing there waiting for me to make sense.
When you were a child, did you have trouble understanding other people’s feelings or intentions?

Well, like I was just touching on a minute ago with the story about Mr. Henderson, no, not at all. I never had any trouble with that. Honestly, I think I was probably better at it than most kids my age. I was always very perceptive. 

Take my mother, for instance. She was a wonderful woman, very stoic, grew up during the Depression so she absolutely never liked to complain about anything, ever. You had to really pay attention to figure out what was bothering her. But I could always tell exactly what she was feeling just by the way she was washing the dishes in the kitchen sink. Our kitchen had this little window right over the sink that looked out into the backyard—which is actually where I first learned to take care of a lawn, helping my dad out there—but anyway, if she was just humming along, washing the plates with a regular rhythm, everything was fine. 

But if she started scrubbing the cast iron skillet... we had this big, heavy black cast iron skillet that we used for Sunday morning pancakes, the kind you are never actually supposed to use soap on, you know, you're just supposed to wipe it out with a paper towel and maybe rub a little oil into it so it keeps its seasoning. But if she was in there actually scrubbing it, clanking it against the porcelain of the sink with a little too much force, I knew immediately that my father had said something at dinner that upset her, or maybe she was stressed about the grocery budget for the week. I didn't even have to ask her what was wrong. I just knew her feelings. I would just quietly walk in, take the dish towel off the oven handle, and start drying the plates, because I understood her intentions and I knew she needed the help but would never actually ask for it out loud. 

So, no, I've never been one of those people who can't read a room or can't understand what someone else is going through. I've always been completely tuned in to other people. It's really just this new thing, like I was explaining before, with the words getting all scrambled up and taking off in different directions when I'm trying to talk to Dave or the cashiers at the store. That is the only thing that's out of the ordinary for me.
Have you had this kind of language or communication difficulty since childhood, or did it begin only recently?

No, no, like I've been saying, my childhood was absolutely fine. I was always a very clear communicator, right from the start. This... this specific issue with the words getting all tangled up and going off the rails, it's entirely recent. 

I'd say the jumbled explanations and those odd stops on the sales floor have been noticeable for about six months now. I can actually pinpoint it pretty well because it was right around the time we were doing our big autumn floor set. Corporate always sends down these incredibly detailed planograms for the seasonal transitions, usually way later than they're supposed to, so we're always scrambling to get the shelving adjusted and the new merchandise out before the weekend rush. 

So, it was about six months ago, and I was out on the floor with Dave—my assistant manager, who I mentioned earlier—and I was trying to explain how we needed to adjust the peg hooks on the main promotional aisle. I was pointing at the shelves, completely focused, and then right in the middle of my sentence, I just... stopped. I had one of these odd stops where the thought just sort of suspended in mid-air. And when I started talking again, instead of finishing the instruction about the peg hooks, I launched into this completely jumbled explanation about the warehouse delivery schedule from three years ago, and something about the tires on my neighbor's car. 

Dave just stared at me with that same scrunched-up look I was telling you about. And ever since that day, for the last six months, it's just become this recurring thing. I'll be walking down the main aisle, clipboard in hand, perfectly ready to give a basic directive to the team, and suddenly I'm giving them these completely scrambled directions that make absolutely no sense to anyone but me in that exact second. It's incredibly disruptive to the workflow, as you can imagine. So, definitely not childhood. It's just been the last half year or so that this has been happening.
When you were in school, did you have trouble learning to read or spell?

No, no trouble at all. Actually, it was quite the opposite. I was always a very strong reader, right from the very beginning. 

I remember back in, oh, it must have been third or fourth grade... let's say third grade, with Mrs. Gable. She was this wonderful older woman who always wore these brightly colored silk scarves, no matter what the season was, and she had this massive reading chart at the back of the classroom. It was pinned up right next to the cubbies where we kept our winter boots, which always smelled like wet wool by February. Anyway, we'd get a little gold star sticker for every chapter book we finished. Well, I had a row of stars so long it actually wrapped around to the next line and started encroaching on the kid next to me on the list, Tommy Miller. I was reading everything I could get my hands on—Hardy Boys, biographies, the encyclopedias my parents bought from a traveling salesman... you name it. 

And spelling, well, spelling was just second nature to me. I actually made it to the regional spelling bee when I was twelve. I'll never forget the word I went out on, though—chrysanthemum. I put an extra 'h' in there somewhere, which was a real shame because my mother actually grew them along the side of the garage, these big beautiful yellow ones that bloomed late in the fall. But anyway, no, I never struggled with the mechanics of language. 

Even through high school and when I went on to get my bachelor's degree, writing papers and reading dense textbooks was a breeze for me. I still read all the corporate memos and the inventory manifests at the store without any issue whatsoever. I can spot a typo on a vendor invoice from a mile away, which actually drives Dave crazy because he never catches them when he's doing the intake. 

So the reading and the spelling, all of that is perfectly intact. The words on the page make total, complete sense to me. It's really just... like I was explaining before, it's just when I try to take the thoughts in my head and push them out of my mouth to explain something to the team on the floor. That's where the disconnect happens, where everything gets all jumbled up. But reading and spelling? No. Never an issue, not in school, not now.
Do you have any repetitive behaviors or unusually strong need for routines, like repeating the same actions, lining things up, or getting very upset when plans change?

Well, it’s funny you mention lining things up, because in retail, lining things up is practically the entire job. We call it "facing" or "blocking" the shelves—you pull all the product to the very front edge of the shelf so the store looks completely full and pristine for the customers. Corporate is incredibly strict about it, especially before a weekend push. So I’ve always been very particular about things looking neat and orderly. 

But getting upset when plans change? No, never. You absolutely cannot survive in retail management if you can't roll with the punches. A delivery truck arrives three hours late, two cashiers call out sick with the flu, the POS system goes down... you just have to deal with it and pivot. 

But as for the repeating actions... I will admit, something strange has been happening in that regard lately. It's not a routine I'm doing on purpose, but... well, sometimes on the sales floor, I'll catch myself just pacing. I'll be walking up and down the exact same aisle, usually the electronics and impulse aisle right up by the front registers, just pacing back and forth. And I'll start straightening the same row of batteries over and over again. You know those little metal peg hooks they hang the blister packs on? I'll just keep adjusting the AA packs, making sure the cardboard is perfectly flush, and then I'll just do it again, and again, just repeating that same motion on the exact same row even though they are already perfectly straight. 

And then there are the times with the clipboard. I always carry this heavy aluminum clipboard—it has a little storage compartment inside where I keep extra highlighters, dry erase markers, and the master break schedule—and I'll walk out to the center aisle, fully intending to get the team organized for the afternoon shift. But then I'll just... stop. I'll just be standing there with the schedule clipboard in my hand, completely still, while the associates are all gathered around waiting for me to tell them what to do. I know they're looking at me, waiting for their tasks so they can get to work, but I just stand there holding the board, kind of stuck in place. It's like my engine is just idling and I can't put it into gear. 

So, I guess I do have these repetitive actions, or these moments where I get stuck doing the same thing, but it's not like a childhood routine or some rigid schedule I need to follow. It's just these weird loops I keep getting caught in out on the floor.
When you speak, do other people say your speech sounds unusual in the way you pronounce sounds or your accent?

No, no one has ever said anything like that. My pronunciation is perfectly fine, actually. I've never had any sort of strange accent or, you know, issues forming the actual sounds of the words. I've lived around here practically my whole life, so I just have a very standard, everyday kind of voice. 

In fact, because my pronunciation is so clear, I'm actually the one they prefer to have doing all the overhead pages on the store PA system. We have this incredibly outdated Cisco phone system that corporate put in maybe ten or twelve years ago—the handset in the main office has a paging button that always sticks if you press it too hard—and the speakers out on the sales floor are so blown out that if you don't enunciate perfectly, it just sounds like pure static. But when I get on there to announce that the store is closing in fifteen minutes and to please bring final purchases to the front registers, or if I have to call for a wet spill cleanup on aisle four, everyone can hear every single syllable I say. It's very crisp. 

Dave, my assistant manager, he actually mumbles quite a bit. He has this habit of swallowing his consonants, especially at the end of a long shift, and I always have to tell him, "Dave, you have to articulate, the stockers in the back room can't hear a word you're saying over the noise of the cardboard baler." 

So no, my actual speech sounds, the mechanics of my voice and my accent, they're completely normal. It's really just the actual meaning of the sentences getting scrambled, like I was telling you with the peg hooks earlier. The words themselves are pronounced perfectly, they just... they just end up being the wrong words entirely. But the pronunciation itself? Completely normal. Nobody has ever had an issue understanding my accent.
When you speak, do other people comment that your tone of voice or intonation sounds unusual or flat?

No, no, I've never heard that. Flat? No, definitely not. If anything, I'm probably a bit too animated sometimes. You see, in retail management, your tone of voice is... well, it's practically one of your main tools. You absolutely cannot have a flat or monotone voice when you're dealing with the general public. Corporate is actually very big on this—they roll out these training modules every single quarter, and the last one was literally called "The Smile You Can Hear." It's all about putting that upward inflection at the end of your sentences so the customer feels warmly welcomed the second they walk through the automatic doors. 

So when I'm at the front of the store, and someone walks in, I don't just drone at them. I say, "Good morning! Is there anything specific I can help you find today?" with this very bright, engaging tone. I've perfected it over the years. And you have to do the exact same thing with the associates, especially on the early shifts. When we're unloading the delivery truck at six in the morning, and the warehouse packed the pallets terribly so all the detergent is leaning dangerously to one side, the team gets frustrated. Dave, my assistant manager, he gets incredibly grumpy in the mornings—he'll just grunt at people and drag his feet. But I have to be the one to rally the troops. "Alright team, let's get this broken down before opening!" You just can't do that if you sound like a robot. You have to project energy and enthusiasm, you have to modulate your voice to keep people motivated and moving. 

So no, my intonation is completely fine. Very expressive, actually. It's exactly like I was saying with the PA system earlier, or with the sentences getting scrambled when I try to give directions. The emotion is there, the tone is there, the volume is there... it's just the actual selection of the words that gets derailed sometimes. But nobody has ever told me I sound flat or unusual in how I express things. Honestly, if I started sounding flat, my district manager would probably write me up for poor customer engagement before anyone even thought to ask if there was something wrong with me!
As a young child, did you have trouble using or understanding gestures like pointing, nodding, or making eye contact?

No, no, definitely not. I never had any issues with that as a kid. My mother actually used to say I was almost too expressive with my hands before I even really started talking in full sentences. I was always pointing at things, making eye contact, nodding along when the adults were talking even if I didn't fully understand the conversation. I've just always been very tuned in to people, you know?

And honestly, it's a good thing I didn't have trouble with that, because gestures and eye contact... well, they are absolutely vital in my line of work. Take eye contact, for example. In retail management, if you can't look a customer in the eye, they immediately think you're hiding something, like you're lying about having extra stock in the back room. We actually train our cashiers on the ten-foot rule. If a customer is within ten feet, you make direct eye contact and smile. I've been doing that naturally my whole life, so training the new hires on it is second nature to me.

And pointing! It is funny you mention pointing, because we actually have a very strict policy about pointing at the store. Corporate calls it the show, do not tell policy. If someone asks where the furnace filters are, you do not just point a finger at aisle twelve. Pointing with one finger is considered aggressive or dismissive. You either use an open-palm gesture to guide their attention, or better yet, you walk them all the way to the aisle yourself. But back when I was a little kid? Oh, I pointed at everything. I would point at the toys in the catalog, I would point at the dogs walking by the house. 

And nodding, too. Nodding is just active listening. When Dave, my assistant manager, when he is complaining to me about the warehouse messing up our pallet delivery again, I am maintaining eye contact, I am nodding, I am letting him know he is heard. I have been doing that since I was in grade school. So no, I never had any trouble understanding or using any of those gestures. I actually have to train the new hires on it, because kids these days, they just want to stare at their phones, they don't know how to hold a real two-way conversation with a living, breathing person standing right in front of them. And it all feels perfectly connected in my head while I'm saying it, like one thought naturally leads right into the next, but then I stop and look at Dave, or the cashiers, and they just have these blank expressions. They look at me like they absolutely cannot follow what I'm saying. Their eyebrows get all scrunched up, and they're just staring at me like I'm speaking a foreign language. It is incredibly frustrating, let me tell you, because like I said before, I have always been the communicator. I've always been the one to give clear directions. target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about childhood difficulties in understanding other people's feelings or intentions, which relates to autism spectrum disorder symptoms. This is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was just touching on a minute ago with the story about Mr. Henderson, no, not at all. I never had any trouble with that. Honestly, I think I was probably better at it than most kids my age. I was always very perceptive. 

Take my mother, for instance. She was a wonderful woman, very stoic, grew up during the Depression so she absolutely never liked to complain about anything, ever. You had to really pay attention to figure out what was bothering her. But I could always tell exactly what she was feeling just by the way she was washing the dishes in the kitchen sink. Our kitchen had this little window right over the sink that looked out into the backyard—which is actually where I first learned to take care of a lawn, helping my dad out there—but anyway, if she was just humming along, washing the plates with a regular rhythm, everything was fine. 

But if she started scrubbing the cast iron skillet... we had this big, heavy black cast iron skillet that we used for Sunday morning pancakes, the kind you are never actually supposed to use soap on, you know, you're just supposed to wipe it out with a paper towel and maybe rub a little oil into it so it keeps its seasoning. But if she was in there actually scrubbing it, clanking it against the porcelain of the sink with a little too much force, I knew immediately that my father had said something at dinner that upset her, or maybe she was stressed about the grocery budget for the week. I didn't even have to ask her what was wrong. I just knew her feelings. I would just quietly walk in, take the dish towel off the oven handle, and start drying the plates, because I understood her intentions and I knew she needed the help but would never actually ask for it out loud. 

So, no, I've never been one of those people who can't read a room or can't understand what someone else is going through. I've always been completely tuned in to other people. It's really just this new thing, like I was explaining before, with the words getting all scrambled up and taking off in different directions when I'm trying to talk to Dave or the cashiers at the store. It was pinned up right next to the cubbies where we kept our winter boots, which always smelled like wet wool by February. Anyway, we'd get a little gold star sticker for every chapter book we finished. Well, I had a row of stars so long it actually wrapped around to the next line and started encroaching on the kid next to me on the list, Tommy Miller. doctor.intent: To determine whether the communication problem is due to a developmental social-communication disorder versus autism spectrum disorder by assessing restricted/repetitive behaviors or sensory rigidity.
doctor.question: Do you have any repetitive behaviors or unusually strong need for routines, like repeating the same actions, lining things up, or getting very upset when plans change?

patient.answer:
Well, it’s funny you mention lining things up, because in retail, lining things up is practically the entire job. We call it "facing" or "blocking" the shelves—you pull all the product to the very front edge of the shelf so the store looks completely full and pristine for the customers. Corporate is incredibly strict about it, especially before a weekend push. So I’ve always been very particular about things looking neat and orderly. 

But getting upset when plans change? No, never. You absolutely cannot survive in retail management if you can't roll with the punches. A delivery truck arrives three hours late, two cashiers call out sick with the flu, the POS system goes down... you just have to deal with it and pivot. 

But as for the repeating actions... I will admit, something strange has been happening in that regard lately. It's not a routine I'm doing on purpose, but... well, sometimes on the sales floor, I'll catch myself just pacing. I'll be walking up and down the exact same aisle, usually the electronics and impulse aisle right up by the front registers, just pacing back and forth. And I'll start straightening the same row of batteries over and over again. You know those little metal peg hooks they hang the blister packs on? I'll just keep adjusting the AA packs, making sure the cardboard is perfectly flush, and then I'll just do it again, and again, just repeating that same motion on the exact same row even though they are already perfectly straight. 

And then there are the times with the clipboard. I always carry this heavy aluminum clipboard—it has a little storage compartment inside where I keep extra highlighters, dry erase markers, and the master break schedule—and I'll walk out to the center aisle, fully intending to get the team organized for the afternoon shift. But then I'll just... stop. I'll just be standing there with the schedule clipboard in my hand, completely still, while the associates are all gathered around waiting for me to tell them what to do. I know they're looking at me, waiting for their tasks so they can get to work, but I just stand there holding the board, kind of stuck in place. It's like my engine is just idling and I can't put it into gear. 

So, I guess I do have these repetitive actions, or these moments where I get stuck doing the same thing, but it's not like a childhood routine or some rigid schedule I need to follow. It's just these weird loops I keep getting caught in out on the floor.

In fact, because my pronunciation is so clear, I'm actually the one they prefer to have doing all the overhead pages on the store PA system. We have this incredibly outdated Cisco phone system that corporate put in maybe ten or twelve years ago—the handset in the main office has a paging button that always sticks if you press it too hard—and the speakers out on the sales floor are so blown out that if you don't enunciate perfectly, it just sounds like pure static. But when I get on there to announce that the store is closing in fifteen minutes and to please bring final purchases to the front registers, or if I have to call for a wet spill cleanup on aisle four, everyone can hear every single syllable I say. Dave, my assistant manager, he actually mumbles quite a bit. He has this habit of swallowing his consonants, especially at the end of a long shift, and I always have to tell him, "Dave, you have to articulate, the stockers in the back room can't hear a word you're saying over the noise of the cardboard baler." 

So no, my actual speech sounds, the mechanics of my voice and my accent, they're completely normal. It's really just the actual meaning of the sentences getting scrambled, like I was telling you with the peg hooks earlier. The words themselves are pronounced perfectly, they just... they just end up being the wrong words entirely. But the pronunciation itself? Completely normal. Nobody has ever had an issue understanding my accent.

No, no, I've never heard that. Flat? No, definitely not. If anything, I'm probably a bit too animated sometimes. You see, in retail management, your tone of voice is... well, it's practically one of your main tools. You absolutely cannot have a flat or monotone voice when you're dealing with the general public. Corporate is actually very big on this—they roll out these training modules every single quarter, and the last one was literally called "The Smile You Can Hear." It's all about putting that upward inflection at the end of your sentences so the customer feels warmly welcomed the second they walk through the automatic doors. 

So when I'm at the front of the store, and someone walks in, I don't just drone at them. I say, "Good morning! Is there anything specific I can help you find today?" with this very bright, engaging tone. I've perfected it over the years. And you have to do the exact same thing with the associates, especially on the early shifts. When we're unloading the delivery truck at six in the morning, and the warehouse packed the pallets terribly so all the detergent is leaning dangerously to one side, the team gets frustrated. Dave, my assistant manager, he gets incredibly grumpy in the mornings—he'll just grunt at people and drag his feet. But I have to be the one to rally the troops. You have to project energy and enthusiasm, you have to modulate your voice to keep people motivated and moving. 

So no, my intonation is completely fine. Very expressive, actually. It's exactly like I was saying with the PA system earlier, or with the sentences getting scrambled when I try to give directions. doctor.intent: Differentiate childhood-onset autism-spectrum social communication differences from acquired language disorder by asking about early nonverbal communication/gestures.
doctor.question: As a young child, did you have trouble using or understanding gestures like pointing, nodding, or making eye contact?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about early childhood deficits in nonverbal communication (gestures, eye contact), which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, no, definitely not. I never had any issues with that as a kid. My mother actually used to say I was almost too expressive with my hands before I even really started talking in full sentences. I was always pointing at things, making eye contact, nodding along when the adults were talking even if I didn't fully understand the conversation. I've just always been very tuned in to people, you know?

And honestly, it's a good thing I didn't have trouble with that, because gestures and eye contact... well, they are absolutely vital in my line of work. Take eye contact, for example. In retail management, if you can't look a customer in the eye, they immediately think you're hiding something, like you're lying about having extra stock in the back room. We actually train our cashiers on the ten-foot rule. If a customer is within ten feet, you make direct eye contact and smile. I've been doing that naturally my whole life, so training the new hires on it is second nature to me.

And pointing! It is funny you mention pointing, because we actually have a very strict policy about pointing at the store. Corporate calls it the show, do not tell policy. If someone asks where the furnace filters are, you do not just point a finger at aisle twelve. Pointing with one finger is considered aggressive or dismissive. You either use an open-palm gesture to guide their attention, or better yet, you walk them all the way to the aisle yourself. But back when I was a little kid? Oh, I pointed at everything. I would point at the toys in the catalog, I would point at the dogs walking by the house. 

And nodding, too. Nodding is just active listening. When Dave, my assistant manager, when he is complaining to me about the warehouse messing up our pallet delivery again, I am maintaining eye contact, I am nodding, I am letting him know he is heard. I have been doing that since I was in grade school. So no, I never had any trouble understanding or using any of those gestures. I have always been very connected in that way, very aware of body language. If anything, I probably read into people's gestures too much sometimes, trying to anticipate what they need before they even ask.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has had difficulty understanding figurative or nonliteral language, which would support an autism-spectrum social communication pattern rather than a developmental language disorder.

patient.answer:
No, no, not at all. Sarcasm is... well, honestly, it's practically a requirement to survive in retail management. If you can't pick up on sarcasm, you are going to have a very, very hard time. I mean, just think about it. When a customer is standing at the customer service desk with a crumpled-up receipt from three years ago and says, "Oh, your return policy is just fantastic," I know they aren't actually complimenting us. I know exactly what they mean. You have to be able to read between the lines and de-escalate. 

And with the staff, too. Dave, my assistant manager, he is probably the most sarcastic person I've ever met in my fifty-nine years on this earth. When we are unloading a truck at five in the morning and it's freezing cold out on the loading dock because the bay doors are jammed again, he'll look at me and say, "Just living the dream, right boss?" He doesn't mean it literally. He's using humor to cope with the miserable conditions. I get that completely. We joke around all the time. You have to, or the stress of the sales metrics and the surprise corporate visits will just eat you alive. 

And figures of speech? Oh, corporate uses those constantly in their emails. They never just say what they mean plainly. It's always, "we need to move the needle on our loyalty card sign-ups," or "let's go after the low-hanging fruit in the seasonal aisle," or "we need to think outside the box to drive foot traffic." I understand all of it. I've been translating that kind of corporate speak for my team for over a decade. 

And like you said, "break a leg"—I actually use that exact one! Before our big Black Friday doorbuster events, when the cashiers are all lined up by the front registers looking completely terrified of the crowd outside, I'll walk down the line and tell them to break a leg. Because dealing with that kind of volume... well, it really is a performance. You are putting on a show for the consumer, keeping that smile plastered on no matter what. So no, I don't have any trouble with idioms or jokes or anything like that. I've always had a pretty good sense of humor, actually. doctor.intent: Determine whether the speech/language difficulty reflects a primary speech disorder versus a broader autism-spectrum social communication profile
doctor.question: When you were growing up, did you have any difficulty understanding how other people felt or what they were thinking?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about childhood difficulties in understanding others' feelings or thoughts (theory of mind/empathy), which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, no, definitely not. If anything, I was probably too sensitive to how other people were feeling when I was growing up. I've always been able to read people like a book. 

I remember when I was just a boy, maybe seven or eight years old, I could always tell exactly what kind of mood my mother was in before she even took her coat off. I would just listen to the way she dropped her keys into the little ceramic bowl by the front door. If it was a sharp, loud clink, I knew she had a terrible day at the office and I needed to just go straight to my room, do my homework, and stay out of her way. But if it was a soft jingle, I knew she was relaxed and I could ask her if my friend Mark could come over to play. I just... I always knew what people were thinking or feeling. I was the kid on the playground who knew exactly who was mad at who, or who was feeling left out of the kickball game, even if nobody said a word. 

And frankly, that intuition is exactly why I ended up in management, and why I've been so successful at it. You simply cannot survive in retail—especially as a supervisor—if you don't know how to read people. It's impossible. When a customer walks through those automatic doors, I can tell within five seconds what's going through their head. I can tell if they are just browsing to kill time because their spouse is at the nail salon next door, or if they are on a mission and are going to get incredibly angry if they can't find the exact model of toaster oven they saw on our website. You have to anticipate their feelings before they even open their mouths. 

It's the exact same thing with the staff. I know what they're thinking before they even clock in for their shift. Like Dave—I know I keep bringing up Dave, but he's my right-hand man—I can tell when Dave is thinking about quitting. It happens about twice a month, usually when corporate sends down a new planogram for the seasonal aisle that makes absolutely no sense and requires us to move heavy shelving units we just set up three weeks ago. I can see it in his eyes, the way his shoulders slump, the way he sighs when he looks at the clipboard. I know exactly how defeated he is feeling in that moment. So I have to step in, read the situation, maybe buy him a terrible coffee from the breakroom machine, and talk him down. 

If I didn't understand how people felt, the whole store would fall apart. The morale would tank, the turnover rate would skyrocket, and the district manager would be breathing down my neck. So, no, growing up, I never had a problem with that. I was always extremely observant of other people's inner lives. Sometimes I think people don't realize how much you can learn about what they're thinking just by watching them for a few minutes. But no, I never struggled with that. Not for a second.

doctor.intent: To determine whether the patient has persistent, lifelong social-communication difficulties typical of autism spectrum disorder rather than an acquired language disorder.
doctor.question: Before these recent speech problems started, did you ever have trouble understanding or using social back-and-forth the way other people do, even as a child?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about deficits in social-emotional reciprocity (a symptom of autism), which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, no, not at all. The back-and-forth, the... the rhythm of a conversation? I've always been completely natural at that. I mean, even when I was a little kid, my parents used to joke that I was a forty-year-old man trapped in a seven-year-old's body because I would just sit at the dinner table and hold court with the adults. My uncle Richard used to come over every Sunday for my mother's pot roast—which, honestly, was always a little dry, but we never told her that—and he and I would just go back and forth for hours. We'd talk about the Mets, or whatever was on the evening news, and I always knew exactly how to keep the ball rolling. You talk, you listen, you respond to what they said, you ask a follow-up question... it's a dance, really. 

And it's a good thing I learned that dance early, because, like I keep saying, retail is entirely built on that back-and-forth. It is the whole foundation of customer service. If you can't manage the give-and-take of a conversation, you are dead in the water. Just last week, I had a woman come in, absolutely livid, just furious because we wouldn't accept an expired manufacturer's coupon for a coffee maker. Now, if you don't understand social back-and-forth, you might just talk over her, or freeze up, or rattle off company policy like a robot. But I know how it works. You let them vent, you give them the floor, and then when they pause to take a breath, you step in with a validation. You say, 'I completely understand why that's frustrating.' Then they say their piece again, maybe a little calmer, and you counter with a solution. 

It's a rhythm. I've been doing it my whole life. I actually have to train the new hires on it, because kids these days, they just want to stare at their phones, they don't know how to hold a real two-way conversation with a living, breathing person standing right in front of them. I have to stand there and explain, 'When the customer says this, you wait, you listen, and then you say that.' But me? No, never an issue. Up until these... these recent speech things you mentioned, my conversational timing has always been absolutely flawless. I've always known exactly how to keep a conversation moving.
